root.title: Geometric Deep Learning: Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges
root.gist: Most deep learning architectures can be derived from a few geometric principles of symmetry, invariance, and scale.
root.question: Geometric Deep Learning — why do so many deep learning architectures share the same underlying structure? (a unifying blueprint)

children.gist: The table of contents listing chapters and sections.

children.title: Preface
children.gist: Following Klein's Erlangen Programme, which unified geometry through symmetry groups, the authors aim to similarly unify deep learning's many architectures under shared geometric principles.
children.question: Erlangen Programme — why apply Klein's symmetry-based unification of geometry to deep learning? (a historical analogy)

children.title: Notation
children.gist: A reference table defining the mathematical symbols used throughout the text.

children.title: 1 Introduction
children.gist: Deep learning's success rests on learning useful features and gradient descent, but exploiting the geometric structure and symmetries of data is key to beating high-dimensional learning's difficulty.
children.question: Geometric Deep Learning — what single framework explains why diverse neural network architectures work? (a unifying principle)

children.title: 2 Learning in High Dimensions
children.gist: Learning generic high-dimensional functions is statistically hopeless, so practical success depends on added structure like regularity assumptions or geometric priors that reduce the effective search space.
children.question: Curse of dimensionality — why does learning in high dimensions require extra structural assumptions? (two mechanisms compared)

children.title: 2.1 Inductive Bias via Function Regularity
children.gist: Neural networks can approximate almost any function, but choosing a regularity measure like weight norm steers them toward simpler, more generalizable solutions among the many that fit the data.

children.title: 2.2 The Curse of Dimensionality
children.gist: Classic regularity assumptions like smoothness require exponentially many samples as dimension grows, and even sparsity-based neural network priors fail when real-world functions have long-range correlations, motivating domain-specific geometric structure instead.

children.title: 3 Geometric Priors
children.gist: Two geometric principles, respecting symmetry and separating scales, let neural networks overcome the curse of dimensionality by building invariant and equivariant functions from first principles.
children.question: Geometric priors — how can symmetry and scale separation make high-dimensional learning tractable? (two principles developed)

children.title: Signals and domains
children.gist: Machine learning systems act on signals defined over a domain, and the geometric structure and symmetry of that domain, as in images or molecules, is what makes learning efficient despite high dimensionality.

children.title: 3.1 Symmetries, Representations, and Invariance
children.gist: Symmetries form mathematical groups whose representations act on data; functions can be built to be invariant (unaffected by the symmetry) or equivariant (transforming consistently with it), the two central properties of geometric deep learning.

children.title: 3.2 Isomorphisms and Automorphisms
children.gist: Different levels of structure, from bare sets to metric spaces, define different symmetry groups as subgroups of each other, and automorphisms (self-symmetries) differ from isomorphisms (equivalences between distinct objects like graphs).

children.title: 3.3 Deformation Stability
children.gist: Because real-world transformations are rarely exact symmetries, functions should instead be stable to small deformations of signals or of the domain itself, a softer requirement than strict invariance that still bounds output change.

children.title: 3.4 Scale Separation
children.gist: Decomposing signals by localized, multiscale wavelet-like filters rather than global Fourier frequencies yields representations that stay stable under small deformations, enabling functions that separate interactions across scales rather than treating the whole domain at once.

children.title: 3.5 The Blueprint of Geometric Deep Learning
children.gist: Combining local equivariant filters, nonlinearities, coarsening operators, and a final invariant pooling layer gives a general recipe that explains how most known geometric deep learning architectures are built.

children.title: 4 Geometric Domains: the 5 Gs
children.gist: Five kinds of structured domains, grids, groups, graphs, geodesics (manifolds), and gauges (bundles), each support their own natural notion of convolution built from their symmetry.
children.question: The 5 Gs — what symmetry structure does each kind of geometric domain supply for building convolutions? (five domains compared)

children.title: The 5 Gs overview
children.gist: The text organizes geometric domains into five families, grids, groups, graphs, geodesics on manifolds, and gauges on bundles, as the recurring structures underlying geometric deep learning architectures.

children.title: 4.1 Graphs and Sets
children.gist: Because graph nodes have no inherent order, functions on graphs must be permutation invariant or equivariant, and local neighborhood aggregation gives a general recipe for building such functions, including on structureless sets.

children.title: 4.2 Grids and Euclidean spaces
children.gist: On grids, fixed node ordering yields translation symmetry instead of permutation symmetry, and classical convolution and the Fourier transform both emerge as consequences of circulant matrices commuting with the shift operator.

children.title: 4.3 Groups and Homogeneous spaces
children.gist: Convolution and Fourier analysis generalize from simple translations to any symmetry group acting transitively on a homogeneous space, as shown through cyclic shifts and spherical rotations, though integrating over very large groups becomes computationally infeasible.

children.title: 4.4 Geodesics and Manifolds
children.gist: Manifolds usually lack a global symmetry group, so convolutions instead rely on intrinsic tools like geodesic distance, parallel transport, and the Laplacian operator's eigenbasis, which stay invariant under distance-preserving isometric deformations.

children.title: 4.5 Gauges and Bundles
children.gist: Because a manifold has no single global reference frame, local frames called gauges can be chosen arbitrarily at each point, and functions must be equivariant to changes of gauge, a symmetry distinct from domain transformations.

children.title: 4.6 Geometric graphs and Meshes
children.gist: Meshes sit between graphs and manifolds, letting researchers define intrinsic, isometry-invariant Laplacians and functional maps that let functions compare signals across differently discretized versions of the same underlying surface.

children.title: 5 Geometric Deep Learning Models
children.gist: Convolutional networks, group-equivariant CNNs, graph neural networks, mesh CNNs, and recurrent networks are all instances of the same geometric blueprint applied to different domains and symmetry groups.
children.question: Geometric Deep Learning models — how does the same blueprint produce CNNs, GNNs, Transformers, mesh CNNs, and RNNs? (five architecture families)

children.title: Models overview
children.gist: The chapter shows how enforcing the geometric blueprint's prescriptions for different domains and symmetry groups recovers nearly all the most popular existing deep learning architectures.

children.title: 5.1 Convolutional Neural Networks
children.gist: CNNs implement the full class of local, translation-equivariant linear operators as convolutions, and innovations like multiscale pooling, residual connections, and normalization explain much of their practical success.

children.title: 5.2 Group-equivariant CNNs
children.gist: Replacing plain translation with a larger discrete symmetry group, such as 3D rotations for medical scans or DNA's reverse-complement symmetry, extends convolution by transforming and stacking filter copies for each group element.

children.title: 5.3 Graph Neural Networks
children.gist: Nearly all graph neural network layers reduce to three flavours, convolutional, attentional, or message-passing, which differ only in how strongly they let neighboring nodes' features interact when aggregating local information.

children.title: 5.4 Deep Sets, Transformers, and Latent Graph Inference
children.gist: Treating a set's nodes as having no edges, a complete graph, or an inferred graph recovers Deep Sets, Transformers' self-attention, and latent graph inference respectively, framing them all as special graph neural networks.

children.title: 5.5 Equivariant Message Passing Networks
children.gist: For molecular graphs with spatial coordinates, message passing layers can be made equivariant to rotations, translations and reflections by depending only on distances between nodes, with richer representations needing irreducible or regular group representations.

children.title: 5.6 Intrinsic Mesh CNNs
children.gist: Mesh convolutions built from geodesic patches must handle the ambiguous choice of local reference frame, either by using isotropic filters, fixing a gauge, pooling over rotations, or building explicitly gauge-equivariant filters.

children.title: 5.7 Recurrent Neural Networks
children.gist: RNNs summarize sequences step by step, and only with appropriately padded sequences and chosen update functions do they achieve a limited form of equivariance to time shifts.

children.title: 5.8 Long Short-Term Memory networks
children.gist: LSTMs add gating mechanisms that fix vanishing gradients and, as shown through a time-warping argument, let gated RNNs flexibly represent dependencies across different time scales that simple RNNs cannot.

children.title: 6 Problems and Applications
children.gist: Geometric deep learning already drives major real-world systems, from drug discovery and protein design to maps, recommender systems, game-playing agents, and medical diagnosis.
children.question: Applications — where has geometric deep learning already made a practical, deployed difference? (a tour of domains)

children.title: Applications overview
children.gist: The chapter surveys influential, though not exhaustive, real-world uses of the five geometric domains across science and industry.

children.title: Chemistry and Drug Design
children.gist: Graph neural networks trained on molecular graphs have found new antibiotics like Halicin and increasingly incorporate rotational and translational equivariance for modeling molecular structure and dynamics.

children.title: Drug Repositioning
children.gist: Modeling drug and biomolecule interactions as graphs lets geometric deep learning repurpose already-approved drugs for new diseases, including against COVID-19, faster than developing entirely new compounds.

children.title: Protein biology
children.gist: Representing protein structure as contact graphs or molecular surface meshes lets geometric deep learning predict protein function and interactions, even enabling de novo design of cancer immunotherapy proteins.

children.title: Recommender Systems and Social Networks
children.gist: Graph neural networks power large-scale recommender systems like Pinterest and Amazon, and can also detect misinformation by modeling how news spreads through user sharing networks.

children.title: Traffic forecasting
children.gist: Modeling road networks as graphs lets graph neural networks predict travel times, a system now deployed at scale in Google Maps and Baidu Maps.

children.title: Object recognition
children.gist: Translation-equivariant CNNs trained on ImageNet drove the broader adoption of deep learning, enabling both accurate image classification and precise, localized object detection and segmentation.

children.title: Game playing
children.gist: Translation-invariant CNNs processing pixel-based game states underpin landmark reinforcement learning successes, from AlphaGo defeating a human champion to MuZero mastering multiple games without known rules.

children.title: Text and speech synthesis
children.gist: Dilated convolutions and Transformers' self-attention surpassed recurrent networks for generating speech and text, enabling systems like WaveNet, BERT, and GPT-3 that power real deployed products.

children.title: Healthcare
children.gist: Geometric deep learning on grids, meshes, and patient or brain-connectivity graphs supports diagnosis tasks from retinal disease detection to neurological disorder prediction from functional brain networks.

children.title: Particle physics and astrophysics
children.gist: Because particle and astrophysical data often take the form of unordered sets or irregular detector geometries, graph and geometric neural networks naturally outperform forcing such data into grid representations.

children.title: Virtual and Augmented Reality
children.gist: Mesh convolutional networks modeling the body or face as a deformable surface enable realistic 3D motion capture and pose estimation, now deployed in commercial augmented reality products.

children.title: 7 Historic Perspective
children.gist: Symmetry has shaped mathematics and physics for centuries, from group theory and Noether's theorem to gauge invariance, and its machine learning uses trace back to early shift-invariant pattern recognition models.
children.question: Symmetry's history — how did the idea of symmetry evolve from ancient philosophy to modern machine learning? (a historical survey)

children.title: Symmetry through the ages
children.gist: From ancient Sumerian designs and Plato's polyhedra to Kepler's analysis of snowflakes, symmetry has long been treated as a path to understanding order and beauty in nature.

children.title: Symmetry in Mathematics and Physics
children.gist: Group theory, developed by Galois, Lie, Klein, and Cartan, became mathematics' language for symmetry, while Noether's theorem linked symmetries to physical conservation laws and gauge invariance later unified the fundamental forces.

children.title: Early Use of Symmetry in Machine Learning
children.gist: Long before modern geometric deep learning, researchers built equivariant pattern-recognition detectors and shift-invariant neural networks like the Neocognitron, laying groundwork that culminated in convolutional neural networks.
